pl-l3d22c4-d1e118.summary: Completes the question: or that man, descended from heaven or is everywhere, as the Son of God or God is said to have come from heaven or to be everywhere.

pl-l3d22c4-d1e121.summary: Answers that if the statement is understood by reference to the unity of person, it can be said soundly; if by reference to the distinction of natures, it is in no way to be granted.
claims: Exchanged predications are true by unity of person, false by distinction of natures.

pl-l3d22c4-d1e125.summary: Quotes Augustine: Christ, God and man, is one person, hence 'no one has ascended into heaven but he who descended from heaven'. By distinction of substances the Son of God descended and the son of man was crucified; by unity of person the son of man descended and the Son of God was crucified, and the son of man was said to be in heaven while speaking on earth. So the God of glory is rightly said to be crucified, though only in the form of a servant, from the weakness of the flesh, not the power of the divinity. The careful reader must discern what is said because of what, and according to what.
claims: By unity of person, the son of man descended from heaven and the Son of God was crucified.
The God of glory was crucified according to the form of a servant, not according to his divinity.
The reader must discern the grounds and respects of predication.

pl-l3d22c4-d1e146.summary: Ends the treatment of the incarnation modestly: let this suffice about the strap of the Lord's sandal, lest the bones of the king of Edom be burned to ash, signaling the limits of inquiry into the mystery.
claims: Inquiry into the incarnation should stop at a fitting limit.

pl-l3d22c4.summary: Asks whether it can fittingly be said that the son of man, or that man, descended from heaven or is everywhere, as the Son of God is said to have come from heaven and to be everywhere. Lombard answers that it can be granted if the statement refers to the unity of person, but not if it refers to the distinction of natures. Augustine explains that because of the unity of person the son of man is said to have descended from heaven and the Lord of glory to have been crucified, though he was crucified only in the form of a servant, from the weakness of the flesh, not the power of the divinity. Lombard then closes the treatment of the incarnation, saying that this should suffice on the strap of the Lord's sandal.
claims: Statements exchanging divine and human predicates hold by reason of the unity of person, not the distinction of natures.
The son of man can be said to have descended from heaven by unity of person.
The Lord of glory was crucified from the weakness of the flesh, not by the power of the divinity.
